title: The Group Plan Rescue
description: Patch a fictional crew's rain-soaked outing with your group: pick fixes, order rescue steps from stated rules, and decide what to keep or cut. Your picks land on a Careful Patch to Quick Pivot scale and a Protect the Main Event to Reinvent the Outing scale.
note: The crew, hall, bus and budget are invented for this game. Fix choices and keep-or-cut picks are playful and unscored; only the three puzzles (two step-ordering tasks and one budget choice) have rules-based answers. Each task stands alone and no budget carries across tasks. This is not a verdict on anyone.

sections.title: Plan Disasters
sections.description: Choose rescue ideas and solve a short budget puzzle.

sections.title: Rescue Order
sections.description: Sequence steps using the stated rules.

sections.title: Keep or Cut
sections.description: Trim the plan to fit.

dimensions.description: Whether you settle a rescue by checking details first or by deciding fast and adjusting along the way.
Whether you try to save the original plan or happily build a new one from what is left.

questions.prompt: Rain cancels the picnic at the park for six friends. What is your group's first fix?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. Moving indoors decides fast while keeping the picnic. Postponing and waiting both check conditions first and protect the original idea. Splitting up reshapes the day.

options.label: Move the whole picnic indoors to a community hall
Split into two mini-plans, one cafe group and one games group
Postpone the picnic to next weekend and keep the date open
Watch the hourly forecast and wait to see if the rain stops

questions.prompt: Two friends text that they will be forty minutes late. How does your group handle the start?
questions.explanation: Each answer is a valid style. Starting now is a quick pivot. Holding everything carefully protects the planned start. A flexible warm-up, or replanning around the latecomers' arrival, reshapes the day.

options.label: Start the first activity now and catch them up when they arrive
Hold everything until all friends are there
Swap in a flexible warm-up activity so latecomers can join midway
Send directions and a meeting stop, then plan the day around their arrival

questions.prompt: Which snack package can the crew afford while keeping every required cost covered?
questions.context: Invented case: the crew has $40 in total. The mandatory hall fee is $15. The crew must also buy six required bus passes at $3 each. After those costs, the crew must choose exactly one snack package. Packages: $7, $8, $9 or $10, as listed in the options.
questions.explanation: The hall fee is $15 and six bus passes cost 6 × $3 = $18. That leaves 40 - 15 - 18 = 7 dollars, so only the $7 package fits.

questions.prompt: The forecast says rain may ease in an hour. How soon should your group lock in the new plan?
questions.explanation: Sliding toward the left means gathering more information first. Sliding right means choosing now and adjusting if conditions change.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to move the picnic into the hall, following every rule in the case.
questions.context: Invented case: The hall fee is $15. Rules: you cannot pay the fee until the hall confirms the room is free. Friends are told the address only after the fee is paid. Games are set up only after the fee is paid.
questions.explanation: Confirming comes first, then payment. Telling friends and setting up both depend only on payment, so either order of those two is accepted.

items.label: Ask the hall if the room is free at 3 pm
Tell the group the hall address
Set up the games on the tables

questions.prompt: Order the steps to get the late friends to the activity, following every rule.
questions.context: Invented case: Rules: a meeting stop can be chosen only after the bus time is known. The stop is announced only once chosen. The first game starts only after everyone has received the announcement.
questions.explanation: Each step unlocks the next: bus time, then the stop, then the announcement, then the game. Only this one order satisfies all rules.

items.label: Check the bus time with the late friends
Choose a meeting stop on the bus route
Send the stop and time to everyone

questions.prompt: The rescued plan is thirty minutes too long. Which trim would your group make?
questions.explanation: Every trim keeps the day workable. Cutting travel or time slices protects the main event, while dropping it reshapes the whole outing.

options.label: Cut the trip to a second spot and keep the main event
Shorten every activity a little so nothing is dropped
Drop the main event and improvise a lighter schedule
Pause to ask each friend which part they value, then trim

questions.prompt: Decide for each item whether your group keeps it or cuts it from the rescue plan.
questions.explanation: Keeping items favors a careful patch of the original plan, while cutting them favors a quick pivot to something new. Neither choice is better.

left.label: Long walk to the second spot

title: Silent Consensus
description: Pass one device around. Each player privately orders lists and picks sides without talking, then the group compares answers to see where you line up and where you split.

sections.title: Order Privately
sections.description: Rank four neutral options each.

sections.title: Pick a Side
sections.description: Choose one of two without discussing.

sections.title: Read the Room
sections.description: Choose what you think others might pick.

dimensions.description: Whether your picks lean toward unhurried, low-energy options or lively, higher-energy ones.
Whether your picks lean toward known, comfortable choices or untried, new ones.

questions.prompt: Order these for a lazy Sunday, from most wanted first to least wanted last.
questions.explanation: Your order shows where you lean on pace and familiarity. Agreement is judged by comparing each player's top and bottom items afterward.

questions.prompt: Order these for a rainy evening in, from most wanted first to least wanted last.
questions.explanation: Rainy-evening picks split between cozy repeats and lively novelty, so rankings here often reveal a clear shared direction or an interesting gap.

items.label: Try a new pop-up food market

questions.prompt: Order these ideas for a team away day, from most wanted first to least wanted last.
questions.explanation: Away-day ideas mix energy and novelty differently, so the group map can show which mix most of you reach for first.

questions.prompt: Pick one for a twenty-minute break, without discussing it.
questions.explanation: A short break is a quick test of energy: stretching outdoors leans lively, while quiet tea leans unhurried.

questions.prompt: Pick one for a group dinner, without discussing it.
questions.explanation: This pair isolates comfort with the known versus curiosity about the untried, a common place for groups to split.

options.label: Try a place nobody has been

questions.prompt: Pick one style for a friends' gift swap, without discussing it.
questions.explanation: Wrapped surprises invite novelty, while wishlist gifts keep things predictable. Matching picks show shared taste for surprise.

questions.prompt: Choose the Saturday-morning activity you would pick. At the end, compare whether the circle lined up.
questions.explanation: This is your own preference. The end comparison shows where the circle's actual answers matched or split.

questions.prompt: Choose the playlist theme you would pick for a shared drive. Compare picks at the end.
questions.explanation: This is your own taste. The comparison shows how the group's actual answers spread.

note: Made for two to four friends or teammates who opt in. Pass the device, answer privately, hide your screen, then compare results aloud. There are no right answers, winners or rankings of people, and results describe only this session.

title: Pack the Group Picnic
description: Solve eight clue-based packing puzzles for four invented picnic guests, matching snacks, seats, bags and gear to people and sharing pairs.

sections.title: Who gets what
sections.description: Match guests and items using the clues.

sections.title: Sharing pairs
sections.description: Pair up gear and find who can share the tent.

sections.title: Final checks
sections.description: Carrying limits and cooler space.

questions.prompt: Match each guest to the snack they will eat. Several guests may share one snack.
questions.context: Invented menu: hummus wraps are dairy-free and filling; cheese sandwiches contain dairy; fruit salad is not a filling meal in this puzzle. Every snack is eaten by at least one guest. Bao avoids dairy and wants a filling option. Celia is the only guest taking fruit salad. Amara and Dev eat the same snack.
questions.explanation: Bao's clues leave only hummus wraps, and Celia has the fruit salad alone. Someone must eat the cheese sandwiches, and only Amara and Dev remain, so they share them.

questions.prompt: Assign each guest to a seating spot without breaking any clue.
questions.context: Spots: shade tent (holds two), camp chairs (hold two), blanket (holds any number). Amara needs shade. Bao cannot sit low to the ground and will not share the tent with Amara. Celia and Dev sit together.
questions.explanation: Amara takes the tent and Bao cannot use the blanket or share with her, so he takes a chair. Celia and Dev would overfill the others, leaving the blanket.

questions.prompt: Choose the bag for each item. Bags can hold several items.
questions.context: Rules, in this order: anything marked keep cold goes in the cooler bag. Otherwise, heavy or hard items go in the backpack. Everything else, being soft and light, goes in the tote.
questions.explanation: The cold rule comes first, so the heavy lemonade still goes in the cooler. The plates are hard and heavy, while napkins are soft and light.

questions.prompt: Give each leftover item to one sharing pair, using all the clues.
questions.context: Pair 1 is Amara and Bao. Pair 2 is Celia and Dev. Each pair gets exactly two of the four items. Amara needs shade. Dev made the sandwiches in the cooler. The blanket is wrapped around the cooler for the trip.
questions.explanation: The tent follows Amara and the cooler follows Dev, and the blanket travels with the cooler. The two-items rule then sends the game set to Pair 1.

questions.prompt: Which pair can share the tent without breaking any clue?
questions.context: The tent fits exactly two people. Amara must be inside it. Celia stays beside the cooler to serve food. Dev owns the speaker, which cannot go in the tent, and he stays with it.
questions.explanation: Amara must be in, and Celia and Dev both have to stay outside. Bao is the only remaining partner. Bao and Celia leaves Amara out.

questions.prompt: Assign each item to a sharing pair so all clues hold.
questions.context: Pair A is Amara and Celia. Pair B is Bao and Dev. Each pair carries exactly two items. The lantern goes to the pair with someone staying past sunset, and only Dev stays past sunset. The lantern and water jug never travel together. The ball set goes to the pair without the water jug.
questions.explanation: The lantern follows Dev to Pair B, so the jug goes to Pair A. The ball set avoids the jug, and the trash bags fill Pair A's second slot.

questions.prompt: Connect each guest to every item they can carry alone without exceeding their limit.
questions.context: Limits: Amara 7 kg, Bao 10 kg, Celia 6 kg, Dev 12 kg. Item weights: cooler 9 kg, tent bag 6 kg, blanket 1 kg, lemonade crate 8 kg. A guest can carry an item if its weight is at most their limit.
questions.explanation: Only Bao and Dev reach the 9 kg cooler and 8 kg crate. The 6 kg tent bag fits everyone, including Celia at exactly her limit, and the blanket fits all four.

questions.prompt: How many drink bottles can still fit in the cooler after the other items are packed?
questions.context: The cooler has 12 slots. Each ice pack takes 2 slots. Each sandwich box takes 1 slot, with one box per guest for four guests. Two ice packs go in. Each bottle takes 1 slot.
questions.explanation: Two ice packs use 4 slots and four sandwich boxes use 4 slots. That is 8 of 12 slots, leaving 4 for bottles.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All guests, snacks, gear and weights in this quiz are invented for the puzzles. Every clue you need is given in each task.

title: Rebuild the Weekend Together
description: Work through a scrambled, invented weekend with your group. Reorder activities from clock, travel and energy clues, then pick the swap that fixes each conflict.

sections.title: Timelines
sections.description: Rebuild three scrambled days from the clues.

sections.title: Swaps
sections.description: Choose the change that resolves each conflict.

sections.title: Final rebuild
sections.description: Combine two parallel tracks into one plan.

questions.prompt: Put these six Saturday activities in a workable order so nobody rushes or misses anything.
questions.context: Invented Saturday for four roommates. Brunch runs 11:00 to 12:00 and is the first time everyone meets. The grocery store is open only 12:00 to 1:00. The hike takes 2 hours and must end before the 5:30 sunset. Everyone showers right after the hike, before cooking. Cooking needs the groceries. The movie starts at 7:00.
questions.explanation: The store closes at 1:00, so the two-hour hike cannot fit before it. Groceries come first, the hike follows, then showers and cooking, with the movie last.

questions.prompt: Rebuild this Sunday so the friends make their train home without skipping anything.
questions.context: Invented Sunday for three friends in a made-up city. Packing must be finished before checkout. Hotel checkout is at 8:00. The market is open 8:30 to 10:00 and takes 1 hour. The museum is open only 10:30 to 12:30 and the visit takes 2 hours. Lunch is booked for 12:45. The train leaves at 4:00 pm.
questions.explanation: The market fits between checkout and its 10:00 close. The museum's only two-hour window is 10:30 to 12:30, which falls before the 12:45 lunch. The train comes last.

questions.prompt: Order Noor's arrival-day plans using the travel times and shop hours given.
questions.context: Invented Friday in a made-up coastal town. Noor's flight lands at 1:00 and she clears the airport by 1:30. The apartment is one hour from the airport. The bike shop is next door to the apartment and stops rentals at 3:00. Nobody bikes with suitcases. The coast ride takes 2 hours and bikes must be back by 5:30. Dinner is at 7:30.

items.label: Pick up Noor at the airport

questions.explanation: Noor arrives at 1:30 and reaches the apartment at 2:30. Bags go down first, bikes are rented before 3:00, the ride follows, and dinner comes after the bikes are returned.

questions.prompt: Which swap lets the group finish the hike and still reach the fixed brunch without rushing?
questions.context: Invented plan: a 2-hour hike starts at 9:00. The brunch table in town is fixed at 11:00 and the drive from the trailhead takes 40 minutes. The trail opens at 7:30.
questions.explanation: An 8:00 start ends at 10:00, and the 40-minute drive arrives at 10:40. The 8:30 start arrives at 11:10 and the 9:00 shorter route arrives at 11:10, both late.

questions.prompt: Which replacement for the dance class keeps Maya's energy from dropping below zero?
questions.context: Invented energy points: Maya starts with 4 and cannot go below 0. Climbing costs 3, dance class costs 3, bowling costs 1, a museum walk costs 2 and karaoke costs 3. The current plan is climbing, then dance class.

options.label: Swap the order of climbing and dance

questions.explanation: Climbing (3) plus bowling (1) uses exactly 4 points. Museum walk totals 5, karaoke totals 6, and changing the order leaves the total at 6.

questions.prompt: Which dinner seating gets everyone to the theater at least 15 minutes before the film?
questions.context: Invented evening: the movie starts at 7:00. Dinner lasts 90 minutes, the theater is a 15-minute walk away, and the restaurant only seats parties at 5:00, 5:45, 6:30 or 7:15.
questions.explanation: A 5:00 seating ends at 6:30, and the walk arrives at 6:45. The 5:45 seating ends at 7:15, already after the movie begins.

questions.prompt: The group wants to keep the concert and stay within budget. Which single swap does that?
questions.context: Invented currency: each person has 60 tokens. Plan: concert 35, dinner 20, bowling 12, total 67. Options replace exactly one item. Food truck costs 15, arcade 10, picnic 18 and park walk 3.
questions.explanation: Swapping bowling for a park walk gives 35 + 20 + 3 = 58 tokens. The other swaps total 62, 65 and 65, all over 60.

questions.prompt: Order this Sunday reset. Two tracks run alongside each other, and guests arrive only when both finish.
questions.context: Invented chores for two housemates. Laundry must be washed, then dried, then folded. Dinner needs vegetables chopped before cooking. Guests arrive after the folding and the cooking are both done. Any order that respects these rules works.
questions.explanation: Laundry and cooking are independent tracks, so they can interleave freely. Only the steps inside each track and the final arrival have to be in sequence.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All weekends, towns, times, energy points and token budgets are invented for this puzzle. Work through the clues together as a group; the score reflects puzzle accuracy only.

title: Two Truths and a Plot Twist
description: Read six invented character dossiers and find the one claim that breaks the facts, then choose fair twists for two new cards. Play together on one device or solo.

sections.title: Spot the Twist
sections.description: Six dossiers, three claims each.

questions.prompt: Which claim about Mira contradicts her dossier?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Mira repairs watches at a shop in the made-up town of Lantern Bay, has no pets, and won first place in the town pie contest.
questions.explanation: The dossier says Mira has no pets, so three cats is the twist. Repairing watches and winning the pie contest both match the file.

options.label: She works as a watch repairer

questions.prompt: Which claim about Dev is the invented twist?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Dev drives a city bus on the night shift, has never owned a car, and sleeps during daylight hours.
questions.explanation: Dev has never owned a car, so commuting in his own car contradicts the file. Driving a company bus does not require owning a vehicle.

options.label: He drives a bus at night
He drives his own car to the depot
He is usually asleep at noon

questions.prompt: Which claim about Ines breaks her dossier?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Ines keeps the lighthouse on the made-up island of Skerry Point, talks to ships by radio, and has never left the island.
questions.explanation: A monthly mainland market trip contradicts never leaving the island. Tending the lamp and using the radio both fit the job described.

options.label: She shops at a mainland market each month
She greets passing ships by radio

questions.prompt: Which claim about Tomas is the plot twist?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Tomas won the Rook Street Chess Club title, has been blind since birth, and plays using a board with raised, notched squares.
questions.explanation: Choosing an opening by seeing the board colors contradicts being blind since birth. Reading the board by touch and winning the title fit the dossier.

options.label: He reads the board by touch
He picked his opening by seeing the square colors

questions.prompt: Mark each claim about Anaya as fitting the dossier or being the twist.
questions.context: Invented dossier: Anaya has lived 200 days in a row aboard the made-up orbital station Kestrel-9. She grows lettuce in water trays and has never handled soil on the station.
questions.explanation: Walking in a park last month conflicts with 200 straight days aboard. Water-tray lettuce and a stay over 150 days both match the file.

cells.label: She walked in a park last month
She grows lettuce in water trays
She has been aboard over 150 days

questions.prompt: Which claim about Rumi's ferry shifts is the twist?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Rumi pilots the ferry on made-up Lake Verra. The ferry sails only on even-numbered dates, and Rumi never works on days it does not sail.
questions.explanation: The 9th is odd, so the ferry does not sail and Rumi would not be piloting. The 14th is even, and being off on the 9th fits.

options.label: She piloted the ferry on the 14th
She piloted the ferry on the 9th
She was off duty on the 9th

questions.prompt: Build round: which new claim makes a fair twist, one players can catch from the dossier?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Kofi guards a museum at night, hates loud noise, and keeps a pet tortoise.
questions.explanation: Hosting drum circles clashes with hating loud noise, so players can catch it. The other claims either match the file or have no clue behind them.

options.label: He guards the museum on night shifts
He hosts weekly drum circles in his flat
He feeds lettuce to his tortoise
He walks the museum halls on patrol

questions.prompt: Build round: which new claim is a fair twist for Lena's card?
questions.context: Invented dossier: Lena captains a tugboat in the made-up Port Alder, wears a red cap every shift, and has never missed a tide.
questions.explanation: Skipping morning tides contradicts never missing a tide. Favorite soup, a scarf, or a sister would be unfair, since the dossier offers no clue about them.

options.label: She often skips the morning tides

note: All characters, places and dossiers are invented for this quiz and are not real people or facts. Play on one device by discussing each card together, or solo.

title: Who Chose That?
description: Each player privately makes eight fictional road-trip picks on one passed device, then the group compares answers and guesses aloud who chose what.

sections.title: Secret pair picks
sections.description: Choose privately, then pass the device.

sections.title: Reveal-round picks
sections.description: Answer privately, then reveal and guess seats aloud.

dimensions.description: Whether your road-trip choices lean toward snug, familiar comfort or open-air, adventurous surprises.
Whether your choices lean toward shared moments for the whole van or time and treats that are just yours.

questions.prompt: Your fictional road trip needs a departure plan. Which pair choice would you make?
questions.explanation: This pick leans on how you picture the start of an adventure. Neither answer is right; it is just a playful clue for the table.

questions.prompt: At a roadside snack stop, which pick sounds more like you?
questions.explanation: Snack choices show whether you reach for something shared or something personal. Your table can guess which seat picked each.

options.label: Buy one favorite treat just for yourself
Buy one big snack box for everybody

questions.prompt: The trip reaches a quiet valley for the night. Where would you sleep?
questions.explanation: Cabin versus tent is a taste in comfort and exposure to surprise, not a skill test or a personality measure.

questions.prompt: The van needs music for a long stretch. Which rule would you pick?
questions.explanation: Taking turns spreads the spotlight, while owning the speaker gives one person control. Both are fine picks for a game.

options.label: You control the speaker for one full hour

questions.prompt: Rank these four detour stops from most to least appealing for you.
questions.context: Fictional detours: a quiet bakery, a cliff-edge trail, a giant roadside map photo stop for the whole group, and a bookshop you browse alone. After revealing, guess which seat ranked each stop first.
questions.explanation: Your top and bottom spots show the mix of coziness, adventure, group time and solo time you lean toward on this trip.

items.label: Group photo at the giant roadside map
Browsing a bookshop on your own

questions.prompt: Plan the final day's energy. Where does your slider land on the trip tempo?
questions.explanation: A slider lets you place your taste between snug and daring. At reveal, guess which seat landed furthest toward each end.

questions.prompt: Match each surprise moment on the trip with the response you would choose.
questions.context: Several moments can share the same response. Pick the reaction you would choose; compare answers after everyone finishes.
questions.explanation: Repeated targets are allowed, so patterns show where you lean when plans change: comfort, adventure, group play or solo time.

left.label: Rain begins during the afternoon drive

questions.prompt: For the last night of the trip, which celebration would you pick?
questions.explanation: The final-night pick wraps up your mix of shared and personal, cozy and bold. Reveal it, then guess which seat chose the other option.

options.label: One big shared dinner for everyone
A solo night-market dash for your own finds

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: Pass-and-play for 2–4 consenting friends. Every trip, detour and place is invented. Each player answers privately, then the comparison shows actual answers side by side. Guessing happens aloud, and the Cozy/Bold and Table/Own scales describe choices only.

title: Friendship Time Capsule
description: Each player privately chooses preferred plans and shared wishes for an imagined future, then the group compares answers at the end of the session.

sections.title: Predictions
sections.description: Pick the outcomes you expect for the group.

sections.title: Wishes
sections.description: Choose goals worth sealing.

sections.title: Reveal
sections.description: Decide how the opening should feel.

dimensions.description: Whether you expect and prefer plans to bend around people or stay pinned to a calendar date.
Whether you lean toward quick, casual get-togethers or larger, planned celebrations.

questions.prompt: Imagine a group trip planned for next spring. Which outcome would you prefer?
questions.explanation: There is no right answer. This is your preference, compared with the other players at the end of this session.

options.label: It happens on the original schedule
It moves whenever it suits everyone
It becomes a relaxed day outing
It moves to a fixed summer weekend for better weather

questions.prompt: For the next group birthday, which celebration would you prefer?
questions.explanation: This is a preference, not a score. Differences at the end comparison are conversation starters.

options.label: A same-day coffee that comes together spontaneously
A short group video call on the day
A weekend away whenever everyone is free

questions.prompt: If the group set up regular meetups, which format would you prefer?
questions.explanation: This shows your own preference. Matching answers are not better or worse than differing ones.

options.label: A recurring calendar invite on a fixed day
Meeting whenever a few people happen to be free
A rotating host who picks a casual hangout
A bigger seasonal gathering instead of monthly ones

questions.prompt: If the group started a shared photo album, which version would you prefer?
questions.explanation: This is about style, not effort. The end comparison shows how differently people picture the same project.

options.label: A one-page collage of small everyday moments
A printed book with chapters for each event

questions.prompt: If your group picked a date to reopen these wishes together, how firmly would you like to keep it?
questions.explanation: This is your preference. Compare slider positions at the end of this session.

questions.prompt: Rank these shared wishes from the one you most want to seal first to the one you want least.
questions.explanation: Rankings show your own priorities and have no correct order. Compare orders at the reveal to find shared favorites.

items.label: Let dates float to fit everyone

questions.prompt: Match each shared goal to the way you would like to seal it in the capsule.
questions.explanation: Many goals can share one approach. These are your own preferences, so there are no right pairs, only pairs to compare.

right.label: Put a date on it now

questions.prompt: When the capsule opens, how big should the reveal moment be?
questions.explanation: Your answer sets the tone you would like for opening. Talk about the differences, then pick a plan the whole group likes.

note: Private pass-and-play for two to four players. Each person answers alone, then the comparison shows everyone's answers. Scenarios are invented prompts, and results describe preferences only, not friendship quality.

title: The Everyone-Wins Tournament
description: Work together through a fictional game-night bracket: four matchups, three semifinals and a final, solving rule-based puzzles about shared wins that leave no loser.

sections.title: Matchups
sections.description: Turn four head-to-heads into shared wins.

sections.title: Semifinals
sections.description: Combine wins into workable plans.

sections.title: Final
sections.description: Choose the closing ritual.

questions.prompt: Snack versus playlist: which category lets both sides win under the bracket rule?
questions.context: Bracket rule: a shared win needs a category where both sides contribute something and neither side is ranked above the other.
questions.explanation: Only the pairing night has both sides contributing equally. The other choices rank one side or remove a side entirely.

options.label: A snack-and-song pairing night where each track gets a matching bite
A loudest-playlist award that outranks every snack
A crown for the snack table, with the playlist as background
A switch-off where the playlist replaces the snack table

questions.prompt: Match each matchup to the category card that needs exactly its two roles.
questions.context: Each card lists the two roles it needs. A matchup fits a card only when the card needs both of the matchup's roles.
questions.explanation: Each card was built around one pair of roles, so a match gives both sides an essential job rather than a rank.

right.label: Open-kitchen supper (needs a cooking role and a tidying role)
Welcome-and-cheer lap (needs a greeting role and a cheering role)
Story circle (needs a telling role and a hearing role)
Rules-and-tally table (needs a tracking role and a ruling role)

questions.prompt: Mark each proposed win as a shared win or as one that creates a loser.
questions.context: A proposal creates a loser if it compares the sides or makes one side judge the other. Otherwise it is a shared win.
questions.explanation: Co-designing and trading halves keep both sides equal. Louder-cheer cups and contribution votes rank the sides, so someone loses.

cells.label: Both teams co-design one menu board
The team with the louder cheer takes the cup
Each side picks half the playlist, then they trade halves
Judges vote on which side contributed more

questions.prompt: Order the matchup ritual so every rule is respected.
questions.context: Rules: a category cannot be named until both sides state their contribution. Co-winners are announced only after the category is named. The card and the cheer both come only after the announcement.
questions.explanation: Contributions come first, then the category, then the announcement. The card and the cheer both follow it, and either may go first.

items.label: Each side states what it contributes

questions.prompt: Which plan fits both wins into the semifinal slot?
questions.context: The slot lasts 60 minutes. Supper Table takes 30 minutes and Story Circle takes 20. Any two consecutive activities need a 10-minute reset between them.
questions.explanation: Supper (30) plus reset (10) plus Story Circle (20) fills exactly 60 minutes. Skipping the reset breaks the rule, and the other plans overshoot.

options.label: Supper Table 30, then Story Circle 20 with no reset
Supper Table 30, reset 10, Story Circle 20, reset 10, a 10-minute encore

questions.prompt: Connect each win to every room that can host it.
questions.context: A room can host a win if it provides at least one thing the win needs. Kitchen: food. Living room: seating. Courtyard: movement. Library nook: quiet. Needs: Supper Table (food, seating); Story Circle (seating, quiet); Cheer Lap (movement); Tally Table (seating, quiet).
questions.explanation: Each win connects to every room that supplies at least one of its needs. Supper Table fits two rooms, Cheer Lap only the courtyard.

questions.prompt: Exactly two of three wins must run in the third semifinal. Which pair works?
questions.context: Wins: Dessert Swap, Lantern Walk, Trivia Duet. Dessert Swap and Lantern Walk need the same helpers, so they cannot both run. Trivia Duet runs only if Lantern Walk also runs.
questions.explanation: Dessert Swap with either other win breaks a rule: it clashes with Lantern Walk, and Trivia Duet needs Lantern Walk. Only Lantern Walk plus Trivia Duet works.

options.label: Dessert Swap alone, with a repeat

questions.prompt: Which closing ritual satisfies every final-round condition?

title: Carpool Seat Puzzle
description: Seat invented friends in cars using seat counts, bag limits and departure clues, then match pickup stops to cars, sort pickup order and check trip arithmetic.

sections.title: Fill the Cars
sections.description: Assign riders to cars using the clues.

sections.title: Match the Stops
sections.description: Decide which car serves each stop.

sections.title: Order and Arithmetic
sections.description: Sequence pickups and check trip numbers.

questions.prompt: Choose the car for each rider so every clue is satisfied and both cars are full.
questions.context: Car A fits four people, Car B fits three, and all seven riders go. Car B is the early departure, and Priya and Leo must leave early. Sam's cello only fits Car A's trunk. Mei will not ride with Sam. Tomas and Jon ride together.
questions.explanation: Priya and Leo fill two of Car B's seats and Sam is in Car A. Tomas and Jon need two seats together, so only Car A works. Mei fills Car B, leaving Amara in Car A.

questions.prompt: Place each rider in Red, Blue or Green so all three cars end up full.
questions.context: Red fits three, Blue fits two, Green fits two, and all seven riders go. Omar's tent poles need Red's roof rack. Nia and Kofi share a car that is not Red or Green. Hana and Diego share a car that is not Red.
questions.explanation: Nia and Kofi can only take Blue. Hana and Diego cannot take Red or full Blue, so they take Green. Red keeps Omar plus the two remaining riders, Yuki and Lena.

questions.prompt: Assign each rider to the Van or Hatchback so seats and trunk space are both used exactly.
questions.context: Each car fits three riders. The Van trunk holds 6 bag units and the Hatchback holds 4; all must be filled exactly. Bags: Ines 2, Ravi 1, Chen 3, Zola 1, Ola 2, Bea 1. Zola rides with Chen. Ines and Ola ride in different cars. Ravi rides with Ola.
questions.explanation: Chen's 3 bags plus Zola's 1 leave room for one 2-bag rider in the Van. If Ola took it, Ravi would make four riders. So Ines joins the Van and Ola, Ravi and Bea take the Hatchback.

questions.prompt: Match each stop to the one car that serves it.
questions.context: Cars leave at fixed times: Car A 7:00, Car B 7:20, Car C 7:40. Car A serves one stop, B two, C two. The ferry dock pickup needs a car leaving 7:40 or later. The library opens at 7:30, so its car leaves 7:20 or later. Bakery and Market are on one street and share a car.
questions.explanation: Only Car C can reach the ferry dock. Bakery and Market need two shared slots, which only Car B has free. The library then joins Car C, leaving the gym for Car A.

questions.prompt: Match each pickup stop to Silver or Teal so every waiting person gets a seat.
questions.context: Silver has 4 free seats and Teal has 5. Waiting people: Museum 2, Pool 1, Station 3, Park 2, Studio 1. Pool and Studio share a building, so one car serves both. Museum and Park use different cars. The Park pickup is at 8:50, after Silver's route ends.
questions.explanation: Park must go to Teal, and Museum goes to the other car. Silver then needs 2 more seats from Pool and Studio together, making 4. Teal takes Station and Park for 5.

questions.prompt: Arrange the four pickups in any order that obeys every rule.
questions.context: Car A collects Dara, Eli, Fatima and Gus. Rules: Dara is picked up before Eli. Eli is picked up before Gus. Fatima is picked up before Gus. No other order is required.
questions.explanation: Gus must come last because both Eli and Fatima precede him. Dara must come before Eli, and Fatima can slot anywhere before Gus, so several orders work.

questions.prompt: How many of the six friends must ride in Car B?
questions.context: Car A fits four seats and Car B fits three. Sam rides in Car A, and his cello takes one extra seat there. All six friends travel and no seat is left empty in either car.
questions.explanation: Sam and the cello use two of Car A's four seats, so Car A carries three people. Six minus three leaves three people for Car B.

questions.prompt: Which car reaches the lake first, and by how much?
questions.context: Car B leaves at 9:10 and drives 35 minutes. Car A leaves at 9:25 and drives 15 minutes. Both drive without stopping.
questions.explanation: Car B arrives at 9:45 and Car A arrives at 9:40, so Car A is five minutes ahead despite leaving later.

Spider plant with window bracket and watering log

cells.label: Waterproof cover for a bike pannier

questions.prompt: Using each price cap, choose who each gift can go to. Prices are in swap credits.

questions.prompt: Match each gift to the recipient whose card it satisfies. Several gifts may share a recipient.
questions.context: Tomás has a small balcony and wants plants. Uma wants things for writing letters by hand. Vik has a long train commute and wants a pastime that needs no power.

left.label: Planter that hangs on a railing

questions.explanation: Pen and paper both serve Uma's letter writing. The railing planter fits the balcony, while the card game and novel need no power for Vik's commute.

questions.prompt: Match each gift-tag note to the gift whose features it describes.
questions.context: Gifts: a clip-on reading lamp with a soft, narrow beam; b seed packets with a sowing calendar; c 1000-piece landscape jigsaw; d deck of handwritten 'open when' cards.

cells.label: Note: Light on the pages, dark for everyone else.
Note: A weekend table project to do together.
Note: Sort the edge pieces first, then fill the middle.
Note: A small message waiting for a rough day.

questions.explanation: The lamp's narrow beam, the jigsaw's edge pieces and table project, and the handwritten cards each match one note. Two notes point to the jigsaw.

questions.prompt: Each note states an intended effect. Which gift delivers it?
questions.context: Gifts: a insulated lunch tote with ice pack; b collapsible umbrella with reflective trim; c wind-up alarm clock with no battery; d soft eye mask.

cells.label: Note: Wake up without a phone or batteries.
Note: Stay dry and noticeable on a dusk walk.
Note: Block daylight while sleeping after a night shift.
Note: Keep packed lunch cool until noon.

questions.explanation: Each effect depends on a single named feature: no battery, reflective trim, blocking light, or an ice pack. No two notes share a gift here.

questions.prompt: Match each tag note to the gift it describes. A gift can match more than one note.
questions.context: Gift a is a set of sticky-tab bookmarks. Gift b is a pocket-size sewing kit with needles and thread. Gift c is a pebble-tray planter for a bright windowsill.

left.label: Fix a loose button before a meeting.
Mark favourite passages without folding pages.
Give a seedling a bright ledge.
Tuck into a bag for a quick repair on a trip.
Hold your place across three books at once.

questions.explanation: Buttons and travel repairs need needle and thread, page marking needs tabs, and the seedling note names a bright ledge, which fits the planter.

questions.prompt: Who receives the scarf? Each person gets exactly one gift, and all clues are true.
questions.context: Wen, Xia and Yara each receive one of: a scarf, a bike bell, a sketch pad. Clues: the sketch pad is not for Xia. The bell goes to someone who rides, and only Xia and Yara ride. The sketch pad is not for Wen.
questions.explanation: The sketch pad cannot go to Xia or Wen, so Yara has it. The bell then goes to Xia, the other rider, leaving the scarf for Wen.

title: Crew Roles Backstage

sections.title: Match the jobs
sections.description: Pair tasks with roles and with certified crew.

sections.title: Cover the gap
sections.description: Pick who can fill a surprise hole.

sections.title: Set up and close
sections.description: Sequence steps using the stated rules.

questions.prompt: Match each backstage task to the role that handles it in this invented school show.
questions.context: Harbor Lane Middle School's spring show is invented. Lights handles lamps and brightness. Sound handles microphones, speakers and audio files. Props handles handheld objects and table items.

left.label: Aim the spotlight at center stage
Set the teapot on the tea table
Fade the stage lamps to blue

questions.explanation: Spotlights and lamp fades are both about brightness, so one role covers both jobs. Microphones belong to Sound, and the teapot is a handheld table item.

questions.prompt: Assign each job to the one crew member who is certified and available for it.
questions.context: Invented roster. Mina: Lights and Sound, Act 2 only. Omar: Props, Act 1 only. Priya: Sound and Props, Act 2 only. Lena: Lights, Act 1 only. Each person takes exactly one job.

left.label: Act 2: cue a lamp change and a headset mic together
Act 2: hand off a prop and check a mic pack

questions.explanation: Each job needs specific certifications in a specific act. Only one person fits each combination, so the roster resolves cleanly.

questions.prompt: For each combined job, choose the set of certifications one person needs to cover it.
questions.context: In this invented crew: Lights is lamps, Sound is microphones, speakers and audio files, Props is handheld objects. A job needs every role it touches.

cells.label: Light a lantern prop and brighten the stage lamp together
Play a thunder audio file while lowering the stage lamps
Carry a tray of cups onstage and clip on a headset mic
Test the speaker in the back hall

questions.explanation: Count which of the three areas each job touches. One role can cover several jobs, but a combined job needs every area it involves.

questions.prompt: The sound desk is empty for Scene 3. Who can fill it?
questions.context: Invented Tuesday crew. Ana: Sound, already assigned to the curtain. Bo: Lights and Props, free. Cy: Props, free. Dee: Lights and Sound, free. The desk needs Sound certification and a free person.
questions.explanation: Ana has Sound but is already busy. Bo and Cy are free but lack Sound. Dee meets both requirements.

questions.prompt: In Scene 5, one person must hand over a lantern and trigger a lamp cue seconds later. Who covers both?
questions.context: Invented crew, all free. Eli: Props. Fay: Lights and Props. Gus: Lights. Hana: Sound and Props. Both jobs must be done by one person, so both certifications are required.
questions.explanation: The handoff needs Props and the lamp cue needs Lights. Only Fay holds both, while the others hold just one of the two.

questions.prompt: In Act 2, someone must swap a prop and run a sound cue. Who is the only fit?
questions.context: Invented Act 2 roster. Ines: Sound and Props, Act 1 only. Jo: Sound, Act 2, free. Kai: Sound and Props, Act 2, already running lights. Mae: Sound and Props, Act 2, free. The person must be free in Act 2 with both Sound and Props.
questions.explanation: Ines is not there in Act 2, Jo lacks Props, and Kai is already busy. Mae is free and holds both certifications.

questions.prompt: Order the opening setup steps. Any order that respects every stated rule is accepted.
questions.context: Invented rules. Tape the floor marks before placing furniture. Place furniture before focusing lamps. Charge mic packs before the mic check. Focus lamps and finish the mic check before the full cue run.
questions.explanation: The floor and lamp steps form one chain, and charging then checking mics forms another. The two chains are independent until both feed the full cue run.

questions.prompt: Order the closing steps after the show. Any order that respects every stated rule is accepted.
questions.context: Invented rules. Announce the house is clear first. Clear the props table before returning props to bins. Return props to bins before locking the cabinet. Turn off the sound desk before powering down the light board.
questions.explanation: The announcement opens everything. Props follow a clear, bin, lock chain, while the equipment steps run separately, with the sound desk off before the light board.

title: Surprise Party Timeline
description: Work through four invented surprise-party timelines by ordering steps from clues, then pick the fix that keeps the secret in four trouble-spot scenarios.

sections.title: Line Up the Steps
sections.description: Use the clues to order each plan.

sections.title: Keep the Secret
sections.description: Choose the fix that protects the surprise.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for Amara's surprise so everything is ready before Amara walks in at 6:00.
questions.context: Clues: the cake is delivered at 5:00. Guests arrive at 5:30. The cake is hidden after delivery but before guests arrive. The decoy text goes out after guests arrive. Lights dim last, just before 6:00.
questions.explanation: Delivery at 5:00 must precede hiding, which must precede the 5:30 arrivals. The text follows arrivals, and dimming the lights is the final step before 6:00.

questions.prompt: Use the countdown clues to order the steps for Grandma Lucía's surprise.
questions.context: Everyone shouts Surprise at 4:00. Guests park 20 minutes before that. The decoy text goes out 10 minutes before parking. Balloons are done 25 minutes before the text. The cake is picked up 30 minutes before balloons.
questions.explanation: Working back from 4:00 gives parking at 3:40, text at 3:30, balloons at 3:05 and cake pickup at 2:35. That makes the order cake, balloons, text, parking, shout.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of Mei's studio surprise using the dependency clues.
questions.context: A gift cannot be wrapped before it is bought. Only the wrapped gift gets hidden. Guests enter once the gift is out of sight. Mei is led in after all guests are inside.
questions.explanation: Buying enables wrapping, wrapping enables hiding, hiding comes before guests enter, and Mei comes in only after guests are inside. The clues form one chain.

questions.prompt: Order the steps for Dara's rooftop surprise. Any order that respects the clues counts.
questions.context: Banner and table setup can happen in either order, but both must finish before guests hide. Lights go off only after everyone is hidden. The shout happens once the lights are off.
questions.explanation: Banner and table are independent, so either may go first, but both precede hiding. After that the chain is hide, lights off, shout.

questions.prompt: Priya is in the Book Club chat, and her phone shows message previews. Which fix keeps the party plans secret?
questions.context: The secret holds only if no party-related message, even a coded one, appears in any chat Priya can read.

options.label: Plan in the Book Club chat using code words
Make a new planning chat that leaves Priya out
Post plans in Book Club, then delete them quickly
Mute the Book Club chat for Priya

questions.explanation: Only a separate chat without Priya keeps every party message out of her sight. Code words, quick deletes and muting by others still leave a visible trail or are not possible.

questions.prompt: The cake delivery window is 5:00 to 6:00 and cannot be narrowed, but Priya gets home at 5:30. What is the fix?
questions.context: Neighbor Ola is home all afternoon and has agreed to accept parcels. The bakery can deliver to any address.

options.label: Send the cake to Ola's address instead
Keep the address and ask the driver to knock softly
Ask Priya to wait outside until 6:00

questions.explanation: Ola receives the cake whenever it arrives in the window, so Priya never sees it. A soft knock or a later window could still collide with her 5:30 arrival.

questions.prompt: Priya leaves the office at 5:00 and the trip takes 30 minutes. Which decoy request lands her home between 6:10 and 6:20?
questions.context: Guests are hidden by 6:10, and snacks must be out by 6:20. Each decoy is a favor that delays her departure from the office.

options.label: Help a coworker with a spreadsheet for 40 minutes

questions.explanation: Forty minutes means she leaves at 5:40 and arrives at 6:10. Twenty minutes gets her home at 5:50, while 60 and 90 minutes push arrival to 6:30 and 7:00.

questions.prompt: Priya's window faces only Elm Street, and she walks home along it. Where should eight guests' cars go?
questions.context: Maple Lane runs behind the building and cannot be seen from Elm Street or from her window. A garden gate opens from Maple Lane into the courtyard.

options.label: Park on Elm Street and walk in quickly
Park on Elm Street and cover the cars with tarps
Park on Maple Lane and use the garden gate
Park on Elm Street but arrive all at once

questions.explanation: Maple Lane is out of sight from both Elm Street and her window. Every Elm Street option leaves cars or people visible on her route home.

title: Roommate Treaty Table

questions.prompt: Guests visit often and one roommate works nights. Which rule would your group adopt first?

options.label: A guest calendar posted by the door
Guests anytime; the night worker gets a door sign and earplugs
No fixed rule; text each other about the week's shifts

questions.prompt: After a lively dinner, dishes cover the counter. How does the treaty handle kitchen cleanup?

options.label: A rotating chore chart on the fridge
Clean as you go, with a quick check-in if it piles up
The kitchen closes to cooking at 11pm
Whoever hosts the meal cleans up after

questions.prompt: The living room is the only shared space. How should the treaty divide it on weekends?

options.label: First come, then talk it out on the spot
Open any night with a volume limit everyone agrees to

questions.prompt: Final clause: rank what matters most in the treaty, from most to least important.
questions.explanation: Ranking turns the treaty into priorities. Higher-ranked items count more toward your two preference scales.

questions.prompt: Last clause: rank how the invented flat should record and renew its treaty, best first.

items.label: A signed page on the fridge
A door sign for rest time
A heads-up text before host nights

Stay at ground level near the door and the pots

Call the others up to look together

Knock on the door and wait to be answered

Rattle the handle and shout hello

Sort the seed packets into neat groups

Sketch the room to work out where a bell could hang

Hold hands and freeze in place
Count the chimes out loud together

title: Five-Minute Group Quest
description: Pass the phone around a short invented adventure: choose a path together at four forks, then solve three team puzzles along your route.

questions.prompt: A lantern flickers where the cave splits. Which way does your group go?
questions.explanation: Both routes are fine story paths. This fork decides which final puzzle your group meets at the last door.

options.label: Light the lantern and climb the left stair
Follow the faint chiming down the right tunnel

questions.prompt: A rope bridge and a narrow stone ledge both cross the gap. Which does the group pick?
questions.explanation: Both crossings reach the same gate. This choice only shapes your story, so there is no wrong answer.

questions.prompt: Put the four runes in the only order that satisfies every gate rule.
questions.context: Press each rune once: Sun, Star, Leaf, Moon. Rules: Moon comes after Leaf. Star comes before Leaf. Sun comes before Star.
questions.explanation: Sun must precede Star, Star precedes Leaf, and Leaf precedes Moon. Chaining the rules leaves exactly one order: Sun, Star, Leaf, Moon.

questions.prompt: Beyond the gate, two doors stand open. Where does your group head next?
questions.explanation: The library and the workshop both lead onward. This is a story choice, so nothing here is scored.

questions.prompt: What code opens the chest? Work it out together before choosing.
questions.context: Three wall torches burn with 3, 5 and 2 flames. The chest code is the total number of flames multiplied by the smallest single torch's flame count.
questions.explanation: The total is 3 + 5 + 2 = 10. The smallest torch has 2 flames, so the code is 10 × 2 = 20.

questions.prompt: A stone fox offers to guard one item through the final hall. What do you leave with it?
questions.explanation: Either item makes a fine story. The fox is just a pause before the last door, and nothing here is scored.

questions.prompt: Match each lantern to the door it opens.
questions.context: A lantern opens the door whose number equals its ribbon count minus one. Amber has 3 ribbons, Teal has 5, Violet has 3. The doors are numbered 2 and 4.
questions.explanation: Amber and Violet each have 3 ribbons, so 3 − 1 = 2 and both open Door 2. Teal has 5 ribbons, so 5 − 1 = 4 opens Door 4.

questions.prompt: Decide how many times each hanging chime rings to open the echo door.
questions.context: A chime rings once for every full 20 cm of its length, ignoring any leftover. Chime 1 is 52 cm, Chime 2 is 35 cm, Chime 3 is 41 cm.
questions.explanation: Chime 1 has two full 20 cm lengths, Chime 2 has one, and Chime 3 has two. Leftover centimetres do not add a ring.

questions.prompt: Tap the spot that shows a guest needs a nut-free snack.
questions.context: Schematic picnic plan, four zones. Rule: a clue must show a specific guest needs food made without nuts.

diagram.title: Picnic blanket plan
diagram.description: A flat schematic of a picnic with four labelled rectangles: top row and bottom row, left and right.

zones.label: Top left: Cupcake box with a card reading 'Lena: nut-free, please'
Top right: Basket of paper napkins
Bottom right: Kite lying on the grass

questions.prompt: Tap the clue showing the party is being kept secret from Mina.

zones.label: Top left: Sleeping cat on the sofa
Bottom left: Houseplant by the window
Bottom right: Closet with a taped note 'Banner for Mina, keep shut'

questions.prompt: Tap the clue showing Tomas probably left the game room only a moment ago.

diagram.description: A flat schematic of a game room divided into four labelled rectangles.

zones.label: Top left: Board game box, lid closed and dusty
Top right: Chair with a mug still steaming
Bottom left: Stack of unused cushions

diagram.title: Top-down room plan

zones.label: Window on the north wall, left side
Door on the north wall, right side

questions.explanation: Southwest means south (bottom) and west (left). The sofa is the only zone in that corner of the plan.

questions.prompt: Using the guest cards, who should receive the nut-free cupcake?
questions.context: Cards: Ava 'loves mango'. Lena 'nuts make me ill'. Omar 'vegetarian'. Zoe 'working late, arriving at 7'.
questions.explanation: Lena's card is the only one mentioning a nut problem. Vegetarian, mango and late arrival are different details.

questions.prompt: Everyone must be hidden 10 minutes before Mina arrives. When must the group hide?
questions.context: Invented timing: Mina leaves work at 5:30 PM and the trip home takes 40 minutes.
questions.explanation: 5:30 plus 40 minutes puts Mina home at 6:10 PM. Ten minutes earlier is 6:00 PM.

questions.prompt: Whose coat hangs on the middle hook, the green one?
questions.context: Three hooks, left to right. Coats: red, green, blue. Owners: Kai, Nia, Rui. The green coat is on hook 2. The red coat is right of the green coat. Nia owns the red coat. Kai's coat is not on hook 1.
questions.explanation: Red is right of green, so red is hook 3 and blue is hook 1. Kai is not on hook 1 and Nia has red, so Kai has green.

questions.prompt: In an invented rival team's search game, how many hidden clues did that team miss?
questions.context: Invented tally for a different fictional game: each of four rooms hides 5 clues. The fictional team found 3, 2, 4 and 1 clues in the four rooms.
questions.explanation: Four rooms with 5 clues each hide 20. The team found 3+2+4+1=10, so 10 were missed.

title: Group Photo Staging Puzzle
description: Place invented friends in a group photo using position, height, pose and light clues, then pick the fix for flawed layouts.

sections.title: Place the People
sections.description: Use the clues to fill every spot.

sections.title: Read the Frame
sections.description: Find the right spot on a schematic.

sections.title: Fix the Layout
sections.description: Choose the change that solves the flaw.

questions.prompt: Fill each spot in the back row, counting from the far left, so every clue is satisfied.
questions.context: Four invented friends stand in one row: Dana, Omar, Priya and Leo. Omar holds the banner and must be in one of the two middle spots. Dana is at the far left. Leo stands immediately right of Omar. Priya is not next to Dana.
questions.explanation: Dana takes spot 1, so Omar is in spot 2 or 3. If Omar is in spot 3, Leo is in spot 4 and Priya lands beside Dana. So Omar is in spot 2.

questions.prompt: Place each person in the two-row photo so no one is hidden behind someone as tall or taller.
questions.context: Invented friends Mina, Tomas, Aiko and Rafi. Heights: Mina is shorter than Tomas, Tomas is shorter than Aiko, Aiko is shorter than Rafi. Each back-row person must be taller than the person directly in front. Rafi is back-left. Tomas is front-right.
questions.explanation: Mina and Aiko remain for front-left and back-right. Mina is the shortest, so she cannot stand behind anyone. Aiko goes back-right, which is taller than Tomas in front.

questions.prompt: Assign each friend exactly one pose so every clue holds.
questions.context: Invented friends Noor, Ethan, Sofia and Kofi each take a different pose: banner, stool, balloons or wave. The banner holder is not Noor or Ethan. Sofia holds neither banner nor balloons. Kofi neither sits nor waves. Noor does not wave. Ethan neither sits nor waves.
questions.explanation: Sofia cannot hold the banner, so Kofi does. Ethan cannot sit, wave or hold it, so he has balloons. Noor cannot wave, so she sits, leaving Sofia to wave.

questions.prompt: Ivy is the youngest and squints in bright sun. Which zone suits her, given the front-row rule?
questions.context: The youngest person must stand in the front row. Squinting happens in open sun, not in shade.

diagram.title: Top-down yard schematic
diagram.description: A schematic rectangle seen from above. The upper half is the back row, the lower half is the front row. A tree's shadow covers the left side; the right side is open sun.

questions.explanation: Ivy needs the front row and shade. Only front-left meets both; back-left is shaded but wrong row, and front-right is the right row in sun.

questions.prompt: Omar's banner should sit as near the 50% centerline as possible. Which unblocked slot should he use?
questions.context: Frame slots are measured left to right as a percentage of frame width. The centerline is at 50%. A lamppost stands in front of the 50–70% slot, blocking it.

diagram.title: Front-view frame with four banner slots
diagram.description: A schematic of the photo frame from the front, widths shown as percentages. Four vertical slots sit across the middle: 4–26%, 28–48%, 50–70% and 74–96%. The 50–70% slot has a lamppost in front.

questions.explanation: The 50–70% slot is blocked. The 28–48% slot ends only 2 points from the centerline, while the outer slots are 24 points away.

questions.prompt: Which single swap fixes the layout so every back-row person clears the 10 cm rule?
questions.context: Invented friends. Front row, left to right: Ana 150 cm, Joel 160 cm. Back row, left to right: Ravi 155 cm, Mei 185 cm. Each back-row person must be at least 10 cm taller than the person directly in front.
questions.explanation: Swapping Ravi and Joel puts Joel (160) behind Ana (150) and Mei (185) behind Ravi (155). Both gaps reach at least 10 cm; the other swaps leave a shorter person behind.

questions.prompt: Which swap keeps every dark outfit out of the backlit spots?
questions.context: Invented friends in one row, spots 1 to 4. Windows are behind spots 2 and 3, so people there are backlit and must wear light outfits. Spot 1 Nia, light. Spot 2 Owen, dark. Spot 3 Pia, light. Spot 4 Quinn, dark.
questions.explanation: Owen moves to spot 1 and light-outfit Nia takes spot 2, so spots 2 and 3 are both light. Every other swap leaves or puts a dark outfit in spot 2 or 3.

questions.prompt: How should the banner move so it is exactly centered in the frame?
questions.context: The frame is 720 px wide. Omar's banner is 300 px wide and its left edge is currently 270 px from the left side of the frame.
questions.explanation: A centered banner has equal margins: (720 − 300) ÷ 2 = 210 px on each side. The left edge is at 270, so the banner moves left by 60 px.

title: Guess the Fictional Crowd
description: Read tiny invented party surveys, add up the tallies, and work out which options won and how they ranked. Eight quick data puzzles for party hosts.

sections.title: Find the winner
sections.description: Pick the most common option in each invented survey.

sections.title: Rank the crowd
sections.description: Order the options from most to least chosen.

questions.prompt: Across all three invented groups combined, which movie-night snack was chosen most?
questions.context: Invented survey, 3 groups. Rooftop: popcorn 4, fruit 6, candy 2. Garden: popcorn 5, fruit 1, candy 3. Loft: popcorn 3, fruit 2, candy 4. No real respondents.
questions.explanation: Totals are popcorn 12, fruit 9 and candy 9. Fruit led only in Rooftop, but the combined count decides the winner.

questions.prompt: Adding both rounds of this invented karaoke survey, which role got the most picks?
questions.context: Invented survey. Round 1: singer 5, DJ 7, hype crew 4. Round 2: singer 6, DJ 3, hype crew 8. Each guest picked one role per round.
questions.explanation: Totals are singer 11, DJ 10 and hype crew 12. DJ won round 1, but hype crew wins once both rounds are combined.

questions.prompt: Which game type was picked most in this invented board-game survey?
questions.context: Invented survey of 40 guests, each picking one type. Co-op games got 12 picks. Bluffing games got 10 picks. Everyone else picked trivia.
questions.explanation: Co-op plus bluffing is 22 picks, so trivia got 40 minus 22, or 18. That beats both of the other types.

questions.prompt: Which dish won this invented potluck survey of 50 guests?
questions.context: Invented survey, one pick each. Salad got 14 picks. Pasta got exactly twice as many picks as dessert. Salad, pasta and dessert were the only options.
questions.explanation: Pasta and dessert share 36 picks. With pasta double dessert, dessert is 12 and pasta is 24, so pasta leads salad's 14.

questions.prompt: Counting each table's top pick, which icebreaker was the most common table favorite?
questions.context: Invented survey of 7 tables. Top pick by table: A would-you-rather, B charades, C charades, D two truths, E would-you-rather, F charades, G two truths.
questions.explanation: Charades topped three tables, while would-you-rather and two truths each topped two. Counting tables, not guests, gives charades the lead.

questions.prompt: Order the drinks from most chosen to least chosen after combining both invented rounds.
questions.context: Invented survey. Round 1: lemonade 15, juice 10, sparkling water 11, iced tea 4. Round 2: lemonade 12, juice 12, sparkling water 7, iced tea 5.
questions.explanation: Totals are lemonade 27, juice 22, sparkling water 18 and iced tea 9. Sparkling water beat juice in round 1 only.

questions.prompt: Using the clues, order the invented dessert survey from most chosen to least chosen.
questions.context: Invented survey. Ice cream got 7 picks. Pie got twice as many as ice cream. Cake got 6 more than pie. Brownies got 3 fewer than cake.
questions.explanation: Ice cream 7, pie 14, cake 20 and brownies 17. Ranked from most to least: cake, brownies, pie, ice cream.

questions.prompt: Order the decoration choices from most picked to least picked in this invented 50-guest survey.
questions.context: Invented survey, one pick each. Lanterns got 40% of picks. Balloons got 30%. Streamers got one fifth. Paper flowers got all remaining picks.
questions.explanation: Of 50 picks: lanterns 20, balloons 15, streamers 10. Paper flowers get the remaining 5, so the order is clear.

questions.context: Invented dinner: the tab is 48 in total, and one shared dessert costs 12. The 36 of other items is split equally among all four friends. The three dessert eaters split the dessert equally.

questions.explanation: A free try shows curiosity. There is no wrong pick; each task simply stretches a different side of how you like to help.

options.label: Announcing the schedule through a megaphone
Labeling every shelf and bin for the next event
Building a welcome sign before doors open
Handing out thank-you notes at the exit

questions.prompt: Swap 3 of 3: if you could be seen or unseen at this party, where would you place yourself?
questions.explanation: Seen and unseen roles both make a party work. This final slider shows how much spotlight you want alongside your finishing choice.
questions.highLabel: Behind the scenes, keeping things smooth

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: The rooftop party, roles and swaps are invented for play. This is a group conversation starter, not a personality test or a prediction of how anyone behaves at real events. Pass one device so each person answers privately, then compare.

title: Icebreaker Ladder
description: Climb a ladder of eight icebreaker prompts, from light to warm. Pick an answer or pass on any prompt, then compare answers with the group.

sections.title: Level 1: Light
sections.description: Easy openers. Skipping is always fine.

sections.title: Level 2: Medium
sections.description: Pick a prompt or swap for a lighter one.

sections.title: Level 3: Warm
sections.description: Gentle, optional reflections.

dimensions.description: How much you lean toward playful, surface-level prompts versus thoughtful, personal ones.
How much you prefer quiet, calm formats versus animated, talkative group energy.

questions.prompt: Would you rather start a meeting with a joke, a playlist or a one-word check-in?
questions.context: Answer privately. Passing is always an option and carries no penalty.
questions.explanation: Any choice is valid. Jokes and playlists tend to raise group energy, while a one-word check-in keeps things calm and brief.

options.label: A joke to get everyone laughing
A shared playlist playing as people arrive
A one-word check-in around the group

questions.prompt: Which style of self-introduction would you enjoy most in a brand-new group?
questions.explanation: Introductions can be silly, story-based or purposeful. Each style sets a slightly different tone for the group.

options.label: My name plus a favorite snack
A quick story from my week
One hope I have for this group

questions.prompt: How lively would you like the opening warm-up to feel?
questions.explanation: Warm-ups range from hushed and calm to loud and animated. Your slider position shows the energy you would pick today.

questions.prompt: For each moment, choose a format you would like to try, or pass.
questions.context: Many moments can share one format.
questions.explanation: Formats shape how much a group shares. Quick rounds are playful, written notes are private, and small circles invite longer talk.

right.label: Quiet written note, shared if you wish

questions.prompt: Pick the medium prompt you would answer, or say you'd prefer something lighter.
questions.explanation: Preferring something lighter is a normal choice. Prompts about wins, lessons or calm places each invite a different depth.

options.label: A small win you are proud of lately
Something you learned from a mistake
A place that feels calm to you

questions.prompt: Rank these prompt types from the one you would most like to answer to the least.
questions.explanation: Your order shows which prompt styles feel most inviting to you. There is no right ranking, and everyone's ladder can differ.

items.label: Describe a habit you are building
Name a value that guides you
Tell a story about a turning point

questions.prompt: What helps you feel welcome in a new group?
questions.explanation: Welcome can come from invitations, structure or space to express needs. Each is a valid preference.

options.label: A clear plan for the session
A chance to say what I need

questions.prompt: What would you like to leave the circle with at the end?
questions.explanation: Closings can be a laugh, a thank-you or an intention. Your pick shows what kind of ending feels right to you.
