note: Pass the device so 2–4 players answer privately, then compare answers. Every prompt is optional and passing is always fine. Choices are tastes, and nothing here judges relationships.

title: Everyone Gets Something Swap
description: Trade items among invented friends: map who wants each offered item, check simultaneous swaps, and spot when no exchange can satisfy everyone.

questions.prompt: Connect each offered item to the person who wants it.
questions.context: Ana offers a scarf and wants a book. Ben offers a book and wants gloves. Cy offers gloves and wants a scarf.
questions.explanation: Cy wants the scarf, Ana wants the book, and Ben wants the gloves. The three arrows form one closed loop, so a simultaneous handoff works.

questions.prompt: Connect each item to every person who would accept it.
questions.context: Dara accepts only the lamp. Eli accepts the kite or the puzzle. Fay accepts only the puzzle. Draw every acceptable link.
questions.explanation: The lamp fits only Dara, the kite fits only Eli, and the puzzle fits both Eli and Fay. Items can have several acceptable recipients.

questions.prompt: Match each offered item to the person who wants it.
questions.context: Kai offers a mug and wants a plant. Lia offers a plant and wants a notebook. Mo offers a notebook and wants a candle. Nia offers a candle and wants a mug.
questions.explanation: Nia wants the mug, Kai the plant, Lia the notebook, and Mo the candle. Together they form a four-person loop.

questions.prompt: Which simultaneous swap gives everyone the item they want?
questions.context: Rae offers jam and wants seeds. Sol offers seeds and wants tape. Tia offers tape and wants jam.

options.label: Rae's jam goes to Tia, Tia's tape to Sol, Sol's seeds to Rae
Rae's jam goes to Sol, Sol's seeds to Tia, Tia's tape to Rae
Rae and Sol swap jam and seeds; Tia keeps tape
Rae and Tia swap jam and tape; Sol keeps seeds

questions.explanation: Rae receives seeds, Sol receives tape, and Tia receives jam. Every other option leaves at least one person with an unwanted item.

questions.prompt: Which set of handoffs satisfies all four people?
questions.context: Uma offers a card and wants a pen. Vik offers a pen and wants a card. Wen offers a cup and wants a map. Xia offers a map and wants a cup.

options.label: Uma and Vik swap; Wen and Xia swap
Card to Wen, cup to Vik, pen to Xia, map to Uma
Uma and Vik swap; Wen and Xia keep their items
Uma and Wen swap; Vik and Xia swap

questions.explanation: The group splits into two independent pairs. Each pair wants exactly what the other offers, so two direct swaps finish everything.

questions.prompt: Which plan satisfies everyone who wants to trade, leaving Bea alone?
questions.context: Yara offers a hat and wants a kettle. Zed offers a kettle and wants a book. Abe offers a book and wants a hat. Bea offers a spoon and does not want to trade.

options.label: Hat to Abe, book to Zed, kettle to Yara; Bea keeps the spoon
Spoon to Yara, hat to Abe, book to Zed; Bea takes the kettle
Hat to Zed, kettle to Abe, book to Yara; Bea keeps the spoon
Yara and Zed swap hat and kettle; Abe keeps the book

questions.explanation: Yara gets the kettle, Zed the book, and Abe the hat. Bea is not part of the loop and keeps the spoon.

questions.prompt: Order these planning steps so each step comes after the information it needs.
questions.context: Arrows need both lists. Checking needs the arrows. The handoff happens only after the check passes.

items.label: Draw an arrow from each item to its wanter
Check each person has one item in and one out
Hand everything over at the same time

questions.explanation: Offers and wants are independent lists, so either can come first. Arrows, then the check, then the simultaneous handoff must follow in that order.

questions.prompt: Can all three people end up with the item they want?
questions.context: Cal offers a pen and wants ink. Dee offers ink and wants a pen. Eve offers a cup and wants ink.

options.label: Yes, through a three-person loop from Cal to Dee to Eve
No, because two people want the only ink
Yes, if Dee gives the ink to Eve and keeps the pen
No, because swaps must always be between exactly two people

questions.explanation: Cal and Eve both want the single ink, so one must be left out. Also, nobody wants Eve's cup. Loops of three or more are allowed.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz scenarios and supplied puzzle data

note: All friends, items and wishes in this quiz are invented for the puzzles. Every rule you need is given in each question.

title: The Lost-and-Found Relay
description: Work through an invented library's lost-and-found log, alone or with others: match objects to owners, check which desks and pickup slots fit, and plan the release order.

questions.prompt: Match each lost object to the owner the clues point to.
questions.context: At the invented Harbor Row Library, Amara, Bo, Cleo, Dev and Esi each lost exactly one of the umbrella, scarf, notebook, keys and water bottle. Clues: Dev's item opens a door. Esi's item holds a drink. Bo's item is worn. The umbrella is not Amara's. The notebook is not Cleo's.
questions.explanation: Dev has the keys, Esi the water bottle and Bo the scarf. The umbrella then belongs to Amara or Cleo, and it is not Amara's, so it is Cleo's. That leaves the notebook for Amara, which agrees with the clue that it is not Cleo's.

questions.prompt: Which desk is allowed to release Cleo's lost object?
questions.context: Cleo, Dev, Amara, Bo and Esi each lost exactly one of the umbrella, scarf, notebook, keys and water bottle. Clues: Dev's item opens a door. Esi's item holds a drink. Bo's item is worn. The umbrella is not Amara's. The notebook is not Cleo's. Item marks: umbrella = large; scarf = soft and small; notebook = paper and small; keys = valuable and small; water bottle = small. Front Desk releases items marked valuable or paper. Rack Desk releases items marked large or soft. Quiet Desk releases items marked small and not valuable.
questions.explanation: The clues give Cleo the umbrella. It is marked large only, so it meets the Rack Desk rule but neither the Front Desk rule (valuable or paper) nor the Quiet Desk rule (small and not valuable).

questions.prompt: Connect each object to every desk that is allowed to release it.
questions.context: Item marks: umbrella = large; scarf = soft and small; notebook = paper and small; keys = valuable and small; water bottle = small. Front Desk releases items marked valuable or paper. Rack Desk releases items marked large or soft. Quiet Desk releases items marked small and not valuable. Draw a link whenever an item meets a desk's rule, even if another desk also fits.
questions.explanation: The umbrella fits only the Rack Desk. The scarf is soft and small, so it fits Rack and Quiet. The notebook is paper and small, so it fits Front and Quiet. The keys are valuable, so only the Front Desk. The water bottle is merely small, so only the Quiet Desk.

questions.prompt: Pick the latest pickup slot each owner can use.
questions.context: Slots start at 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00. An owner can use a slot when its start time falls inside their free window, endpoints included. Free windows: Amara 9:30 to 11:00; Bo 11:00 to 12:00; Cleo 10:00 to 10:30; Dev 10:30 to 12:30; Esi 9:00 to 12:30. Ignore how many people share a slot.
questions.explanation: Amara's window ends at 11:00, which counts, so 11:00 is her latest. Bo can reach 12:00. Cleo's window closes at 10:30, so only 10:00 works. Dev and Esi both reach 12:00, since 12:00 is inside 10:30 to 12:30 and 9:00 to 12:30.

questions.prompt: Connect each owner to every pickup slot they can use.
questions.context: Slots start at 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00. An owner can use a slot when its start time falls inside their free window, endpoints included. Free windows: Amara 9:30 to 11:00; Bo 11:00 to 12:00; Cleo 10:00 to 10:30; Dev 10:30 to 12:30; Esi 9:00 to 12:30.
questions.explanation: Amara reaches 10:00 and 11:00. Bo reaches 11:00 and 12:00. Cleo reaches only 10:00. Dev reaches 11:00 and 12:00 but not 10:00, which is before 10:30. Esi's long window covers all three slots.

questions.prompt: Put the five booked pickups in the order the library releases them.
questions.context: Booked pickups: umbrella at 10:00 from the Rack Desk; scarf at 12:00 from the Rack Desk; notebook at 10:00 from the Front Desk; keys at 11:00 from the Front Desk; water bottle at 12:00 from the Quiet Desk. Release rule: earlier slot first. Within the same slot, Front Desk before Rack Desk before Quiet Desk.
questions.explanation: 10:00 first, with the notebook (Front Desk) before the umbrella (Rack Desk). The keys follow at 11:00. At 12:00 the scarf (Rack Desk) precedes the water bottle (Quiet Desk).

questions.prompt: Dev wants the earliest usable slot. Which slot and desk should the library book?
questions.context: Dev's item is the one that opens a door; the items are an umbrella, a scarf, a notebook, keys and a water bottle. Item marks: umbrella = large; scarf = soft and small; notebook = paper and small; keys = valuable and small; water bottle = small. Front Desk releases items marked valuable or paper. Rack Desk releases items marked large or soft. Quiet Desk releases items marked small and not valuable. Slots start at 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00. Dev is free from 10:30 to 12:30, and a slot is usable when its start time falls inside the window, endpoints included.
questions.explanation: Dev's item is the keys, which are valuable and so go through the Front Desk only. His window starts at 10:30, so 10:00 is out and 11:00 is his earliest usable slot.

questions.prompt: Each slot can serve at most two owners and everyone first picks their earliest usable slot. Which owner at the crowded slot has no other slot to move to?
questions.context: Slots start at 10:00, 11:00 and 12:00. An owner can use a slot when its start time falls inside their free window, endpoints included. Free windows: Amara 9:30 to 11:00; Bo 11:00 to 12:00; Cleo 10:00 to 10:30; Dev 10:30 to 12:30; Esi 9:00 to 12:30. Earliest usable slots put Amara, Cleo and Esi at 10:00, and Bo and Dev at 11:00.
questions.explanation: Three owners at 10:00 is one too many. Amara can also use 11:00, and Esi can use 11:00 or 12:00, but Cleo's window closes at 10:30, so 10:00 is her only slot.

note: The library, owners, objects, desks and slots are all invented for this puzzle. Every rule and every piece of data a task needs is shown in that task, and answers are checked only against those rules. You can work through it alone or talk it over with others.

title: The Last Bow at Lantern Theatre
description: Share the archive of a fictional theatre, separate a costume’s maker from its wearer, and uncover the visitor’s name, permissions and unfinished recognition. Includes unscored creative turns.

questions.prompt: Before the group opens the theatre archive, choose who will read the first clue aloud.
questions.explanation: This is a group preference. No reading style is more correct.
questions.context: Original ghost story: Lantern Theatre has been closed for decades. Each Halloween, one seat unfolds and an unseen visitor takes a bow. Tonight volunteers reopen the theatre for a public archive reading. Your group arrives early, before the public, to examine the records. Share one device and take turns reading; with fewer readers, cycle through the turns.

options.label: Take turns reading a sentence each

questions.prompt: Reader 1: reconstruct tonight’s three rehearsal events before the public audience entered.
questions.explanation: The cue test preceded the replica-costume delivery, which preceded the publicity photograph. Together the scraps establish a sequence without relying on clock calculations.
questions.context: Tonight’s three notes: the cue-test log says the empty-seat bow happened during the test. The replica-costume receipt says the delivery came after that test but before the publicity photograph. The photograph’s caption says the public audience was still waiting outside.

questions.prompt: Reader 2: connect each person's contribution to the object the archive can actually credit to them.
questions.explanation: The archive distinguishes making, carrying and painting. Being photographed holding a prop does not establish who made it.
questions.context: Workshop note: Mara Roe sewed the blue velvet coat; Elin Vale made the paper lantern. A backstage photograph shows Miles Reed carrying that lantern while wearing Mara's coat. The scenery receipt credits Miles with painting the sea backdrop.

questions.prompt: Reader 3: whose missing credit best fits the visitor's two clues?
questions.explanation: The cloth clue points to the coat maker; the second clue rules out the performer photographed wearing it. Both are needed to distinguish maker from wearer.
questions.context: The visitor's words appear on a dusty mirror: ‘Find me in the cloth, not in the face that wore it.’ The workshop note credits Mara with sewing the coat; the photograph shows Miles wearing it. Elin made the lantern.

options.label: Elin Vale, who made the lantern
Mara Roe, who sewed the coat
Miles Reed, who painted the sea

questions.prompt: Creative turn: choose how your group would invite the visitor to stay for the final scene.
questions.explanation: This contribution is unscored. Choose a welcome to say aloud; it does not generate or alter the later story.

options.label: Leave a seat open and read softly
Stand together and offer a formal introduction
Have each person speak one word of the welcome

questions.prompt: Reader 4: what does the newly opened correspondence establish about the coat?
questions.explanation: The loan and letter establish permission, and the reference to working in the wings places Mara backstage on opening night. They do not settle what she intended for every future performance.
questions.context: A signed workshop slip lends the blue coat to Miles for opening night. In a separate letter to him, Mara writes: ‘Wear it. I will be in the wings, looking after the seams.’ Neither document discusses later performances.

cells.label: Miles took the coat without Mara’s permission
Mara expected to work backstage on opening night
Mara intended never to attend a later performance

questions.prompt: Imagine finding one more record. Which discovery would most weaken the group’s identification of the visitor?
questions.explanation: The maker is the crucial link. A reliable correction to that attribution would weaken the identification; more evidence of who wore the coat would not settle who made it.
questions.context: Your current identification depends on Mara being the maker of the coat, rather than the performer who wore it. The mirror’s clue refers to the hands behind the cloth. These are hypothetical discoveries, not new facts in the story.

options.label: Another photograph of Miles wearing the same coat
A second programme that repeats Miles’s performer credit
A verified workshop correction crediting the coat’s sewing to Elin instead of Mara

questions.prompt: The group reads ‘Costumes: Mara Roe.’ The empty seat folds, the visitor takes one last bow, and the theatre falls quiet. What would your group put in the programme's final line?
questions.explanation: The story ends with the maker's name restored. Your optional ending line is a creative contribution, not a correct-answer test; it is not saved or sent for analysis.
questions.context: Original fictional ending. All clues and the resolution were authored for this experience; this is not a claim about a real theatre or haunting.
questions.hint: Say a line together, or leave this blank. You can thank the unseen work behind a performance.

sources.label: Original TypologyQuiz fictional scenes, clues and descriptive mappings

note: An original, non-graphic ghost mystery. One group, one shared attempt: take turns reading clues and agree on answers, or play solo. The optional ending line is not saved. This is an authored story, not a generated narrative.

title: The Ferry Between Two Promises
description: Two ghosts wait on opposite shores. Read a cancelled crossing, a kept house key and two unfinished welcomes to discover why neither stopped waiting. Solve together, then choose an ungraded final line.

questions.prompt: What should your group investigate first to explain the repeated crossing?
questions.explanation: Both figures attend to the arriving boat rather than its route or name. Their empty-handed waiting makes an undelivered exchange the strongest lead, without yet revealing what it was.
questions.context: Original fiction. Every Halloween an empty ferry crosses Bellwater Reach. On the west steps, Jonah rises when it docks. On the east steps, his sister Ada does the same. Each holds out a hand, then lowers it when nobody steps ashore. Neither tries to board. Your group has the old ferry office for one night.

options.label: What each waiting figure expected to receive from the other shore
Whether each figure is trying to keep the ferry from sailing
Whether the crossing reenacts a passenger’s final voyage

questions.prompt: Why is the unopened envelope stronger evidence of an interrupted delivery than of Jonah refusing Ada’s message?
questions.explanation: The office is on the east shore with Ada. The letter never acquired the west-shore delivery mark, and the crossing was cancelled. Those details establish interruption; they do not establish a refusal by its intended reader.
questions.context: Original story fragment. Inside the east-shore office is an envelope addressed to Jonah at the west orchard. Ada signed it. The receipt says it was accepted for the final westbound sailing; the delivery space is blank. Beside it, ferryman Lio’s dated log records a broken cable and cancellation of that sailing. The envelope remains sealed.

options.label: It contains a request that Jonah had already answered
Its journey stopped on Ada’s side before it could reach Jonah
Its paper is older than the cancellation notice

questions.prompt: Match each person to the immediate aim best supported by their actions that night.
questions.explanation: Ada invests in a future across the water; Jonah prepares a welcome at home; Lio tries to carry a message without using the damaged ferry. Their aims can coexist even though their plans fail to meet.
questions.context: Original story fragment. Ada had already sent her drawing tools to an east-side mapmaking apprenticeship. Jonah set two places at the west orchard’s kitchen table and left the outside light burning. Lio tied the ferry out of service, then gave the envelope to a road traveller; the traveller returned it after finding the road flooded.

right.label: Find another way to carry the letter
Make room for a return home

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the journey of Ada and then her message, from these records.
questions.explanation: Ada must reach the east counter before signing its receipt. That receipt then accompanies Lio’s road request. Her own crossing succeeded; the message’s return journey did not.
questions.context: Original records. Ada began the afternoon at the west orchard. Her later receipt carries her signature, written at the east office counter. Lio’s request to the road traveller encloses that receipt and explains that the only ferry is now tied up with a broken cable.

items.label: Lio entrusts the envelope to a traveller trying the road
Ada hands in the envelope at the east office
Ada travels from the orchard side to the east shore

questions.prompt: What does the key add to the meaning of Ada’s departure?
questions.explanation: A future elsewhere and a way back can exist together. Keeping the household key complicates Jonah’s interpretation of a permanent rejection; it does not cancel Ada’s new work.
questions.context: Original story fragment. Earlier that day the siblings argued. Jonah’s unsent note remembers Ada taking her trunk and assumes she wanted no further tie to the orchard. But inside Ada’s coat the group finds her old house key, wrapped in a fresh label in her hand: Keep for visits. Her apprenticeship travel papers are still beside it.

options.label: She meant Jonah to sell the orchard immediately
She had abandoned the apprenticeship before it began
She wanted leaving to remain compatible with belonging at home

questions.prompt: Step into each sibling’s position: which crucial fact was missing from what they could know that night?
questions.explanation: The two papers were never exchanged. Jonah could see a departure but not the invitation across the water; Ada could invite him but could not see his prepared place at home. The player knows more than either sibling did.
questions.context: Original story fragment. The group finally opens Ada’s undelivered letter: she asks Jonah to come east before her morning coach, so they can part without the argument as their last conversation. Jonah’s unsent west-side note invites her to supper and says he will keep a place ready. Neither paper reached its reader that night.

cells.label: Jonah, waiting at the west orchard

options.label: Ada wanted him to visit the east landing before the coach
Ada had taken her trunk away from the orchard
The orchard kitchen had a place set for her

cells.label: Ada, waiting on the east shore

options.label: Her new work was on the east side
Jonah had left a place for her at supper
She had asked Jonah to meet before the coach

questions.prompt: Which discovery resolves both siblings’ mistaken versions of the goodbye?
questions.explanation: The letter and supper place answer different fears: Jonah was invited into Ada’s departure, and Ada still had a place at home. Neither invitation required them to choose the same life. The cancelled delivery let both mistake silence for rejection.
questions.context: Original story fragment. When the two papers are laid side by side, the ghosts finally speak. Jonah remembers only the departing trunk; Ada remembers the empty bench beside her at the east landing. Lio has kept the envelope all these years. Your group can now explain the empty hand each sibling offered the ferry.

options.label: Ada’s invitation proves Jonah had agreed to join the apprenticeship
Jonah’s supper place proves Ada had promised to abandon her journey
Each had made a welcome that the other never learned about

questions.prompt: Choose a final line your group would place beside the ferry bell—or select “Keep the silence” and leave it unwritten.
questions.explanation: There is no correct inscription. These lines place different emphasis on the same resolved story; your choice does not change its ending or your accuracy score.

options.label: A door can stay open after someone leaves
The water carried two different versions of goodbye
There was room at both tables
Keep the silence; add no line

questions.context: Original ending, the same for every attempt. Lio reads Ada’s letter toward the west and Jonah’s note toward the east. Ada lifts her house key. Jonah takes down the untouched second cup and carries it onto the ferry. For the first time, someone is aboard when it crosses. At the east steps, the siblings sit together until the morning coach bell sounds. When your group looks again, only the cup remains.

sources.label: Original fiction: The Ferry Between Two Promises, including all letters, observations and records

note: An original, non-graphic ghost story. Suggested cooperative pass-and-play: share one device, take turns reading the next fragment aloud, discuss and submit one shared answer. There are no private player turns, hidden roles or branching outcomes. Solo play also works. The final creative choice is ungraded.

title: The Second Seat at Lantern Hall
description: At a candlelit masquerade, a second place card appears for someone already at the table. Follow the pencil marks, a displaced screen, and two conflicting accounts to learn what the extra chair was meant to show.

sources.label: Original fictional Lantern Hall masquerade story and clues

note: One person can play alone or a group can read clues aloud and agree on one shared answer. The mystery has one fixed ending; the final line is an unscored creative response, with no private turns or branches.

questions.prompt: Mara is sitting at the table, yet a second card bearing her name stands beside an empty chair behind a gauze curtain. Which first reading deserves investigation?
questions.context: Wind rattles the north shutter and stirs the gauze. The host says the extra chair was added that afternoon. A guest assumes Mara is being moved; Mara says no one told her that.

options.label: A second Mara must have entered the hall
The chair proves Mara has higher rank than everyone else
Someone may have planned to move Mara without telling her
The duplicate card can only be a printer error

questions.explanation: The unexplained duplicate could reasonably look like a social slight. The evidence is not yet enough to call it a ghost, a rank, or a printing error.

questions.prompt: A new clue changes what the second card might mean. Which question would best test the snub theory?
questions.context: On the back of the duplicate card Mara finds a pencil note: “At the bell, look toward the curtain.” A thin rectangle of clean floor sits where a small lamp normally stands.

options.label: Who moved the lamp, and what would its light reach?
What brand of ink was used?
Does the empty chair have a higher number?

questions.explanation: The note directs attention to a timed visual event. A moved lamp offers a physical way to test it, while arrival order and ink do not explain the curtain.

questions.prompt: Match each clue to the interpretation it changes most. These clues are discovered before anyone lifts the curtain.
questions.context: The duplicate card points toward the curtain at the bell; the lamp has moved; Mara still has a place at the main table.

right.label: Something is meant to be seen at a particular moment
A movable object may be part of the effect
She was not simply removed from dinner

questions.explanation: The main-table place weakens a simple exclusion story. The note supplies timing, and the floor mark points to moved equipment.

questions.prompt: What does the discovery behind the curtain most strongly suggest?
questions.context: Behind the gauze is a cut-paper silhouette of a seated figure. It is clipped to a stand facing the lamp. From the table, the silhouette can line up with the empty chair.

options.label: The host barred Mara from the table
The paper figure fell there by accident
The extra chair is part of a planned shadow effect

questions.explanation: The lamp, cutout, gauze, and chair together explain how a second seated figure could appear. The hardware does not establish why it was prepared.

questions.prompt: Put the physical steps in the order needed for the silhouette to seem to sit in the empty chair.
questions.context: The stand holds the cutout behind gauze. The moved lamp shines toward it; diners look through the gauze from their seats.

items.label: The cutout blocks part of that light
Its shadow falls on the gauze
From the table, the shadow aligns with the spare chair

questions.explanation: The apparent second diner is a sightline effect: lamp, cutout, screen, then viewpoint. This reconstructs the trick without making it supernatural.

questions.prompt: How should the group now read the host’s account and Mara’s note together?
questions.context: The host says the shadow was planned as a surprise. Mara says she added this line to the duplicate card later: “Ask me about the north window before you light it.” The cutout faces that window.

options.label: The note proves the host meant to frighten Mara
A planned illusion acquired a later caution about the window
Mara’s note says the shadow was never planned
The window note proves the second diner was real

questions.explanation: The shadow apparatus can be a planned effect while the later note is a separate warning. Neither account alone explains the whole card.

questions.prompt: At the bell, what does the group finally learn about the extra chair?
questions.context: Before the lamp is lit, Mara checks the north shutter and catches its loose latch; the shutter could have swung through the lamp’s new position beside the curtain. Mara had cut the silhouette for the planned effect, then added the warning. The host knew about the shadow but had missed the back of the card.

options.label: It was a plan to remove Mara from dinner
The silhouette proves a second person appeared
The eerie second diner was planned; Mara’s later note prevented the lamp from being lit beside the loose shutter
The host invented the window problem to excuse a prank

questions.explanation: The staged shadow explains the duplicate place. The later note and loose latch explain why Mara wanted the window checked before the lamp was used.

questions.prompt: The lamp stays unlit, but the party keeps the paper figure on its stand behind the gauze. Choose a final line for the hall’s guestbook. There is no keyed answer.

title: The Fox Hood at the Costume Exchange
description: Read a fictional costume-exchange desk together. A familiar fox hood goes missing from its return hook; trace its ticket, repair, and the detail its wearer wants to keep.

sources.label: Original fictional costume-exchange desk, borrowed fox hood, repair evidence and handoff.

note: Original fiction for one shared screen or read-aloud play. Seven deductions have fixed keys; the final wording choice is ungraded.

questions.prompt: Which desk rule decides whether this fox hood belongs on the free-to-take rail?
questions.context: Exchange rule: blue tickets mean a garment may be borrowed for the evening and must return; orange tickets mean it is donated. The fox hood has blue ticket 42. A handwritten card says “for Mina after the walk.”

options.label: Ticket colour controls whether it can leave the return system
Any handwritten card makes the garment a donation
A garment becomes a donation whenever its hook is empty

questions.explanation: Ticket 42 is blue, so the hood remains a borrowed item even if it moves off the hook for repair.

questions.prompt: The hook is empty. Which station is the strongest next stop?
questions.context: The return sheet says ticket 42 came back with a loose left ear. A repair slip, written after check-in but with its ticket number smudged, describes a fox hood with crooked green stitching on that ear. The free rail log records only ticket 18.

options.label: The repair table, where the seam and loose ear match two details
The free rail, because another fox hood is recorded there
The exit, because an empty hook means somebody left with it

questions.explanation: The repair slip joins two distinctive details from the returned hood. An empty hook alone cannot establish where it went.

questions.prompt: Three details are recorded at the repair table. Match each to the question it helps answer.
questions.context: Mina remembers the old crooked green stitching on the left ear. The volunteer has spare orange thread but has not yet sewn it. The blue ticket remains pinned inside.

right.label: Will Mina recognize this as the familiar hood?
What new material might alter its look?
Must the garment be returned after borrowing?

questions.explanation: The familiar seam identifies the hood, the spare thread is a proposed change, and the ticket keeps its borrowing status clear.

questions.prompt: The volunteer offers to replace the crooked green seam with tidy orange stitches. What question should be settled first?
questions.context: Mina’s note asks to wear “the fox with the funny green ear” again. The seam holds, but it looks uneven.

Can the volunteer make the orange stitches faster?
Would an orange ear look brighter in a photograph?

questions.prompt: Arrange the desk actions into a handoff that respects both the ticket rule and Mina’s note.
questions.context: The hood is at the repair table. Desk policy requires checking its identity before altering the cloth. Mina’s note must guide the seam finish; the pickup shelf is for completed repairs.

questions.explanation: The identity check and reading Mina’s note may happen in either order. Both come before mending; the completed repair then goes to pickup.

questions.prompt: A visitor saw a fox hood on the free rail. Which two records distinguish that sighting from Mina’s hood?
questions.context: The desk handled two fox hoods tonight. One was donated on orange ticket 18; Mina’s was borrowed on blue ticket 42. A repair slip later records the green-stitched left ear.

The free-rail log is later than the return sheet, so it must concern the same hood

questions.explanation: The two ticket records separate the donated hood from Mina’s borrowed one. A shared fox shape is not an identity match.
